name: The six temperaments (carita)

definitions.definition: Vism III p. 101-114: the six temperaments (cariyā) are the greedy, the hating, the deluded, the faithful, the intelligent and the speculative (fourteen counted by some with combinations, but in brief six). Faith is near-kin to greed, understanding to hate, speculation to delusion. The text gives five means of discerning temperament (posture, work, eating, seeing, the arising of states), then what suits each (lodging and the rest), and which of the forty subjects suit each; it cautions that its discernment of marks is by the teachers' opinion and not essential (p. 107), and that the assignment of subjects is by direct opposition and extreme suitability (p. 114).

name: The forty meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna)

definitions.definition: Vism III p. 110-114: the forty are ten kasiṇas, ten foulnesses, ten recollections, four divine abidings, four immaterial states, one perception (repulsiveness in nutriment) and one defining (of the four elements). The text decides them in ten ways: by enumeration; by what brings access or absorption (ten bring only access); by kind of jhāna; by transcending (of factors or of object); by increase (only the ten kasiṇas are to be enlarged); by object (twenty-two have a counterpart sign, twelve intrinsic-nature states, six objects not to be described; eight moving objects at the preparatory stage); by plane (the ten foulnesses, body-mindfulness and nutriment-perception do not occur among devas); by taking (nineteen by sight, breathing by touch, the air kasiṇa by sight and touch, eighteen by hearing); by condition; and by suitability to temperament.

definitions.definition: Vism IV p. 141-146: sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse and doubt are the unwholesome states from which the first jhāna is secluded; they are the adversaries and opposites of the jhāna factors (concentration/sensual desire, rapture/ill will, applied thought/sloth and torpor, happiness/restlessness and remorse, sustained thought/doubt); the jhāna does not arise while they are unabandoned. Each obstructs in its own way (p. 146).

definitions.definition: Vism IV p. 139-147: the first jhāna, on the earth kasiṇa, is 'secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unwholesome states, with applied and sustained thought, rapture and happiness born of seclusion'; it has five factors abandoned (the hindrances) and five possessed (applied thought, sustained thought, rapture, happiness, one-pointedness), is good in three ways (beginning, middle, end) and has ten marks. Absorption lasts a single moment of consciousness.

definitions.definition: Vism IX p. 295, 318-319: loving-kindness, compassion, gladness and equanimity; each has a mark, function, manifestation, proximate cause, success and failure, a common and a special purpose, and a near and a far enemy (see prc:brahmavihara-bhavana). The beginner starts with loving-kindness, reflecting first on the danger in hate and the benefit of patience.

definitions.definition: Vism XXII p. 682-684: the ten fetters, so called because they bind beings to aggregates, to the fruit of kamma and to suffering; five higher (lust for fine-material and immaterial existence, conceit, restlessness, ignorance) and five lower (personality view, doubt, adherence to rites and observances, sensual lust, ill will). The text says personality view, doubt, adherence to rites and observances, and the sensual lust and ill will that lead to states of loss are cut by the first path knowledge; the remaining gross sensual lust and ill will by the second; the subtle by the third; the five higher by the fourth.

definitions.definition: Vism XXII p. 694: abandoning by substitution of opposites (tad-aṅga-pahāna) is the abandoning of each state by a factor of knowledge that is its opposite; the text pairs, for instance, defining mentality-materiality with personality view, discerning conditions with the view of no cause, seeing arising with the annihilation view, seeing passing away with the eternity view, and lists eighteen principal insights each abandoning one thing (contemplation of impermanence the perception of permanence, and so on).

name: Remedies for resentment in the development of loving-kindness (Vism IX)

definitions.definition: Vism IX p. 298-306 gives the ordered remedies: return to loving-kindness for the earlier persons; recall the Buddha's advice; recall a calm quality in the person or compassion; admonish oneself in verse; reflect on ownership of kamma; recall the Teacher's earlier patience; reflect on the beginningless round; reflect on the benefits of loving-kindness; analyse into elements; share gifts.
